newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN still refuses to clear Iraq on dangerous arms.
newsitem.headline: UN still refuses to clear Iraq on dangerous arms.

text.p: After five years of scrapping weapons of mass destruction, Iraq may still be hiding small but highly significant quantities of banned arms, the United Nations said on Friday.
In a major half-year report to the Security Council, the U.N. Special Commission in charge of Iraqi disarmament said Baghdad needed to make a clear decision to hand over those arms it still retained.

It said it "continues to believe that limited, but highly significant quantities (of arms) may remain, as Iraq has not been able to account for a number of proscribed missiles and certain high-quality chemical and biological warfare agents."

The report prepared by commission chairman Rolf Ekeus covered chemical, biological and ballistic weapons. Nuclear arms are evaluated by the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency, which has not reported any new discoveries.

For example, Ekeus harshly criticised Iraq's six purported final declarations on germ warfare to date. "Major sections are incomplete, inaccurate or unsubstantiated. Materials acquired for proscribed activities are understated," he said, adding that he had not yet received a full account of "weapons produced and destroyed unilaterally."
"Iraq still needs to take a fundamental decision to give up what they still retain and it is clear that they have not done that yet," deputy chairman Charles Duelfer said.

A clean bill of health by the commission is a key requirement by the U.N. Security Council before the embargo on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted entirely. Iraq has been under stringent sanctions since its invasion of Kuwait in 1990.

The report also sought to refute Iraqi charges that Ekeus was deliberately holding back certification for political reasons while praising Iraq for its substantial cooperation in revealing weapons destroyed to date.

Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf lashed out at the commission in an Oct. 2 speech to the U.N. General Assembly, saying it was influenced by American and British intelligence. He noted it had sent 373 inspection teams with 3,574 inspectors to Iraq over more than five years.
"What has this huge army of inspectors been doing for all this long period of time? They did not come to Iraq for a vacation," he said.

But Ekeus in the report said Iraq had a history of concealment that had "put obstacles in the way of rapid completion of the implementation tasks." He added: "The commission has therefore not yet reached the stage where it can state with confidence that everything that is proscribed to Iraq has been identified and disposed of."

On chemical weapons, he said much of the destruction took place between June 1992 and May 1994 when the U.N. helped dispose of more than 127,000 gallons (480,000 litres) of live chemical agents, 28,000 chemical munitions and about 500,000 gallons (2 million litres) of 45 precursor chemicals.
The report said the commission now had a "fundamental understanding" of Iraq's tactical chemical arms but "the most technologically advanced programmes remain unaccounted for."
On ballistic missiles, the commission destroyed 48 operational missiles, 14 conventional warheads, six mobile missile launchers and other equipment.

Ekeus said he believed most missiles had been uncovered but he said Iraq's accounting was not yet complete. He did not say how many missiles remained, although last year he said there were 6 to 15 still in Iraq.
He said the commission had spent $120 million in its activities since April 1991.
